items.title: Give us all a share of Rolls-Royce’s profits | Brief letters
items.standfirst: Government should invest, not subsidise | Size matters | ‘Ferritin face’ | Train announcements | Reform UK’s newspaperRather than give Rolls-Royce a £1.25bn subsidy to develop the next-generation narrow-body jet airliner programme (Nils Pratley on finance, 29 October), would it not be more advantageous to the Treasury, and thus the taxpayer, me included, to invest £1.25bn in shares in the company? That way, we all get a share of the prospective profits, and in the long run pay lower taxes. Patrick Billingham Brighton, East Sussex• You say the Rothbury estate covers “an area the size of Athens” (Wildlife Trusts hit £30m target to buy and rewild huge Northumberland estate, 30 October). John Hubbard Chislehurst, Kent Continue reading...

clusters.neutral_headline: ‘The nipple touch of doom’: what is sad nipple syndrome and what causes it

items.title: ‘The nipple touch of doom’: what is sad nipple syndrome and what causes it?
items.standfirst: People everywhere are searching for the reason behind their sudden bursts of anguish or homesicknessWomen: was your autoimmune condition misdiagnosed?Some say it feels like a sudden burst of anguish; others liken it more to homesickness. The sudden onset of a sinking, upsetting feeling due to nipple stimulation is anecdotally known as Sad Nipple Syndrome (SNS), and for Sandra, it can be triggered by something as commonplace as putting on a shirt.“I was probably a child when I first noticed: ‘Why does touching my nipple make me sad?’” says the 28-year-old. The sensation seemed to happen at random, and without the words to describe it, she kept it a secret. It wasn’t until college that she worked up the courage to Google it. “I realized I wasn’t crazy,” she says. Continue reading...

items.standfirst: Hope Haven in Whitehaven is one of six trial open-access, 24/7 schemes in England offering preventive careThe night Tamara first walked through the doors of Hope Haven, a new community mental health hub in the heart of Whitehaven, she was afraid. “Terrified, actually,” she says. “Like, my life was falling apart. I didn’t know how to stop it from hurting.”The 22-year-old, who works in children’s transport, had been in and out of therapy and counselling since she was 14, after being abused by an acquaintance as a child. After a lengthy legal process her abuser was sentenced, but the “mental challenge” of dealing with what had happened to her was not over. Continue reading...
